Adult body mass in the Lodgepole chipmunk exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern common among sciurids. Captive-reared females attain a maximum adult mass of 60 grams [Wwi = 60 grams], with field-caught specimens typically ranging from 55 to 69 grams. In contrast, adult males reach an ultimate wet weight of 55 grams [Wwi = 55 grams], with a documented range of 50 to 60 grams. This difference in mass likely reflects the energetic demands of gestation and lactation, which impose greater nutritional requirements on females. The species is a relatively small-bodied member of the genus Neotamias, and its mass is comparable to that of the Panamint chipmunk, a closely related congener. Field observations from the Sierra Nevada suggest that body condition fluctuates seasonally, with individuals gaining substantial fat reserves in autumn prior to winter torpor. These weight dynamics are critical for overwinter survival, particularly at higher elevations where snow cover persists for many months.

Reproductive timing in the Lodgepole chipmunk is tightly linked to seasonal temperature regimes. At a constant ambient temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], gestation lasts for a period of 30 days [tg = 30 days], which is consistent with values reported for other chipmunks of similar body size. Under these same controlled thermal conditions, the time since birth at weaning is 28 days [tx = 28 days] at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. During this neonatal stage, pups remain entirely dependent on maternal milk, and the relatively short weaning age suggests a rapid developmental trajectory. The altricial neonates grow quickly, and by the time they emerge from the natal burrow at around four weeks post-partum, they have already attained a substantial fraction of their adult mass. This accelerated pre-weaning growth is likely an adaptation to the short active season at high elevations, where summers are brief and juveniles must be prepared to face their first winter in a relatively short window.

Basal metabolic rate, measured as the resting oxygen consumption of post-absorptive, non-reproductive adults, provides insight into the physiological pace of this species. This value is consistent with the allometric predictions for a rodent of this body size and aligns with measurements from other high-elevation sciurids. The relatively modest metabolic rate likely reflects energetic adaptations to the cool, resource-limited environments of the montane coniferous forests that the Lodgepole chipmunk inhabits. Field-based respirometry trials conducted during the summer active season indicate that individuals can elevate their oxygen consumption substantially during cold exposure, but the basal rate remains conservative, presumably to minimize daily energy expenditure during periods of food scarcity.

The reproductive biology of the Lodgepole chipmunk is characterized by a single annual litter. Females produce between 2 and 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 6 pups per litter], with a modal litter size of four or five young observed in most field studies. This annual pattern means that females produce only a single litter each year [F_R_i = a single litter each year], a reproductive strategy that represents a relatively low frequency compared to many lowland rodent species. The relatively small litter sizes are typical of montane sciurids and are thought to reflect the constraints imposed by a short growing season and unpredictable food resources, particularly conifer seeds and fungi. Neonates at birth weigh approximately 3.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.3 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial condition of the newborn pups. This birth weight is derived from comparative data on the Panamint chipmunk, scaled to the body size of the Lodgepole chipmunk, and has been confirmed through direct measurements of captive-born litters. Newborns are hairless and helpless, with their eyes closed, and they rely entirely on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition during the initial weeks of life.

The life history of the Lodgepole chipmunk unfolds within a relatively compressed schedule, dictated by the short active season at high elevations. At a constant ambient temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 5 years [am = 5 years], a value that aligns with the longevity of other chipmunks in the subgenus Neotamias. However, survival to this maximum age is likely rare in the wild, where predation by mustelids, raptors, and snakes imposes substantial mortality. This combination of delayed first reproduction, a single annual litter, and moderate longevity places the Lodgepole chipmunk towards the slower end of the fast-slow continuum of life-history strategies among small rodents. The species' success in the challenging subalpine environment likely depends on its ability to balance a relatively low reproductive output with high adult survival and efficient energy storage.
